title: Tips to be more efficient with AI?
author: jakeyboypol
selftext:
Hi guys and girls,

I'm new to building games with AI. As of this week, I've started to create a Roblox game just for me to try things out.  
I'm using ChatGPT Astra with a Plus plan because it's something I'm already paying for because of work.

As of right now, my setup is the ChatGPT desktop app connected to Roblox Studio, Obsidian that works as some sort of KB, and Blender for some models that I am not able to make inside Roblox Studio.

All goes well except 1 thing - my credit usage. It takes me about 30m-1h to deplete the 5hour usage limit. And I feel like I am not doing anything crazy. A small low-poly model of a any object takes like 50% of this limit, which feels crazy to me. Then with the coding around and other stuff, I'm basically instantly depleted.

So what are your tips to be more efficient? Better prompts? What model and plan do you guys use? I'm just interested in anything that could help me improve on my path.

Thanks!

comments.author: caesium23
comments.body: LLMs are not meant for 3D modeling, so it doesn't surprise me they'd be wildly inefficient at it. Either learn Blender or use an actual mesh generation model, like Hunyuan or Trellis.

comments.author: mikaeelmo
comments.body: On a Claude Max (x5) plan, using Fable 5.2 at Medium, without subagents, one thing at a time, I find that is a good way of working with a model which is smart enough to do game development (coding and directing asset generation) but rarely hits the 5 hours usage limit. When I need to do lots of work in parallel, I do Fable 5.2 at medium/high with 2 or 3 Opus 5.5 medium/high subagents, depending on the difficulty of the tasks. By limiting the number of subagents like that I might still hit the 5 hours limits, but not too early. Not sure what are the equivalent models for OpenAI these days.

comments.author: Heath_co
comments.body: I suggest working with the AI to through all the settings in the Claude app, and all the commands that Claude has access to, and then use them to maximise token efficiency.

comments.author: Severe-Doctor1951
comments.body: using Astra with the desktop app? try disabling auto-retry on failed requests, it's eating tokens silently and blowing through your budget fast.

comments.author: marvriley
comments.body: There's a make cool button you can setup in Blender.

comments.author: dreadpirater
comments.body: Have Astra write plans that you turn around and hand to Sol to execute.

comments.author: deeek
comments.body: I would try Claude. I find that Opus 5.5 works wonders with Blender and the usage is not terrible with the $20 plan.

comments.author: ef0uro
comments.body: I use a combination of the Claude Max (5x) plan and GPT Pro, dividing the workload between them. Instead of assigning overly broad tasks in one go, I break the workflow into smaller steps—it yields much faster and more accurate results.

comments.author: Project_Asura
comments.body: Use Claude instead of codex trust me

comments.author: burnsbert919
comments.body: Don't use Astra for everything. Save it for the hardest pieces and lean on Sol/Medium for most things, and go even lower for unchallenging tasks. Astra (especially at higher thinking levels) is just crazy expensive.

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body:
stay on light models until you know the task is too complex for the light models

astra is good but it uses up a lot of usage

you have to deal with the same situation with claude too

it comes down to experience imo

comments.author: Tiny_Original3761
comments.body:
Model choice matters less than how much rework you trigger. A few things that cut our usage a lot:

* Don't have the chat model build meshes. Every edit regenerates geometry as code, and that's where your 50% goes. Use a mesh generator or Blender, and let the AI only import and place the result.
* Work in stages, and stop at the end of each one. Something like: design doc → greybox → asset list → swap in models → polish. Tell it to stop when a stage is done and tell you how to test it. Don't let it run ahead into three things at once.
* Greybox first. Build the whole game with boxes and capsules, and keep how things look in one place (an id → builder function). Then swapping in a real model later doesn't touch gameplay code, and you don't burn tokens re-explaining the game.
* Keep a short progress file (done / decided / next) and a rules file the agent reads at the start of every session. A fresh session that reads two short files is much cheaper than one that rereads the whole project or a giant chat history.
* Commit after every stage that works. When something breaks, roll back instead of asking it to dig itself out.
